newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS - S&P gives S.Africa cautious bill of health.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - S&P gives S.Africa cautious bill of health.

text.p: Influential U.S. rating agency Standard and Poor's gave South Africa a cautious bill of economic health on Thursday, but investors remained edgy as the rand took a fresh dive.
S&P affirmed the country's long-term foreign currency credit rating at BB plus -- one notch below investment grade -- an outcome analysts said was the best that could be expected.
"Given the recent turmoil in our financial markets it's good that they are not considering a downgrade," said Dennis Dykes, chief economist at Nedcor bank in Johannesburg.
Economists polled by Reuters last month had predicted that the rating would be unchanged.

S&P, which also held its rating for South Africa's domestic debt at BBB plus, said the outlook for both ratings was positive, supported by the government's commitment to fiscal and monetary discipline set out in its macro-economic strategy.
The country also had a manageable level of debt, low inflation and strengthening political stability, 2-1/2 years on from the first all-race elections, it said.

But any improvement in credit ratings would hinge on implementation of market-friendly policies laid out in the medium-term economic plan -- notably on the budget, exchange control liberalisation and privatisation.

"Until such time as we are seen to be making material progress in implementing the macro-economic package we cannot expect our ratings to change," said Sandra Gordon, economist at fund management company Syfrets in Cape Town.

In the meantime, South Africa will remain vulnerable to speculative flows of funds, reflecting its reliance on confidence-sensitive portfolio investment and its failure to attract significant foreign direct investment.
On the foreign exchange market the rand fell to a seven-week low of 4.5640 bid against a strong dollar on Thursday and technical analysts said the charts pointed to further weakness.
No fresh fundamental factors were seen behind the latest slide in the currency, which has tumbled from 3.65 against the dollar since mid-February.

But economists said investors remained concerned about the country's current account deficit and precariously low reserves which slipped again in September, despite some hopes that the situation might be stabilising.
"I think the rand will still be under pressure until we see reserves being rebuilt," said Gordon.

Traders said the Reserve Bank was in the market to try to support the rand, although the central bank had limited resources given that the reserves had shrunk to 10.04 billion rand ($2.20 billion), representing one month's import cover.
The rand hit an all-time low of 4.59 against the dollar on August 19.

European credit rating agency IBCA was the first to reassess South Africa's country risk following this year's slide in the rand. It announced in June it was holding its long-term foreign currency rating at BB while local currency debt was assigned BB.
Moody's Investor Services Inc rates South African foreign curency debt at an investment grade Baa3 and rand-denominated debt at Baa1.
